t: Maximize Score of Numbers in Ranges — Binary Search on the Answer
o: We pick one integer from each of n intervals [start[i], start[i]+d] so that the minimum pairwise difference is as large as possible. In example 1 the intervals are [6,8],[0,2],[3,5]; picking 8,0,4 yields gaps 8,4,4 so the score is 4. In example 2, picking 2,7,13,18 gives minimum gap 5. Key observation: after sorting intervals by their left endpoint, an optimal selection can be made in increasing order — each chosen number is the smallest value that keeps a candidate gap m from the previously chosen number. Constraints (n up to 1e5, values up to 2e9) rule out any polynomial-in-value search, but feasibility for a fixed gap m is checkable greedily in O(n log n), so we binary search on m.
k: If a minimum gap m is achievable, any gap smaller than m is too — the answer is monotone, enabling binary search.

a.i: Sort intervals by left endpoint. To test gap m, sweep left to right keeping the last chosen value prev; the next choice must be at least prev+m and within its interval, so choose max(prev+m, start[i]). If that exceeds start[i]+d, gap m fails. Binary search the largest feasible m.
s: Feasibility check: greedily place each pick at max(prev+m, start[i]); fail if it exceeds start[i]+d.
a.t: O(n log n log V) — sorting plus ~31 binary-search iterations each doing an O(n) greedy sweep.

w: Binary search on the answer with a greedy checker is the canonical pattern here. Pitfalls: forgetting to sort first, integer overflow when adding d (use 64-bit in C++/Java), and the upper bound (max span divided by n-1). Edge cases: d = 0 forces overlapping intervals (answer 0 unless n... with d=0 all picks equal start[i], so duplicates give 0). Follow-ups: maximize the minimum gap online, or handle weighted picks.
